Managing Complex IBS: A Multidisciplinary, Mechanism-Based Approach
  • Source: Gastroenterology (2026), Vol. 170
  • Topic: Irritable Bowel Syndrome - Diagnosis and Multidisciplinary Treatment
  • Authors: Chang L, Bedell A, Smith J, Smith S, Lembo A
1. Patient Case Overview
  • 50-year-old woman with long-standing, progressive GI symptoms
  • Toxic shock syndrome at age 23 → subsequent intermittent postprandial diarrhea
  • Ages 32-36: Domestic violence during contentious divorce → chronic stress
1.1. Gastrointestinal Symptoms
  • Abdominal pain and bloating (most days per week)
  • Mixed bowel habits: hard stools 25%, loose/watery stools 50%
  • Alternating constipation (3-4 days) → diarrhea
  • Postprandial epigastric discomfort and early satiety
  • Partial relief with avoidance of dairy and wheat
1.2. Medical Comorbidities
  • Hypothyroidism (treated, no impact on bowel habits)
  • Secondary adrenal insufficiency (low ACTH with normal imaging)
  • Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement
  • Possible fibromyalgia with diffuse musculoskeletal pain
1.3. Psychosocial History
  • Childhood sexual and emotional abuse
  • Ongoing family stress (son's recreational drug use)
  • Second marriage with supportive husband
  • Intermittent psychotherapy engagement
  • No diagnosis of anxiety or depression
  • Marked functional decline with chronic fatigue
1.4. Diagnostic Evaluation
  • Routine labs, celiac serologies, fecal calprotectin → unrevealing
  • HLA typing performed
  • Upper endoscopy with gastric/duodenal biopsies → normal
  • Colonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsies → normal
  • Autoimmune, rheumatologic, mast cell testing → unrevealing
  • H. pylori not present in gastric biopsies
  • Cross-sectional abdominal imaging → normal
  • Breath testing: elevated hydrogen (SIBO + fructose malabsorption)
  • Two courses of rifaximin → minimal, transient relief
1.5. Physical Examination
  • BMI 17.5 kg/m² (low)
  • Mild left lower quadrant tenderness
  • Digital rectal examination unremarkable
2. Diagnosis Framework: Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction (DGBI)
2.1. Irritable Bowel Syndrome Diagnosis
  • IBS with mixed bowel habits (IBS-M) diagnosis
  • Hard stools >25% + loose/watery stools >25%
  • Chronic symptoms >3 months with onset >6 months before diagnosis
  • Meets Rome criteria for IBS
2.2. Overlapping Functional Dyspepsia (FD)
  • Postprandial epigastric discomfort and early satiety
  • Unrelated to bowel habits
  • Fulfills FD criteria: chronic bothersome postprandial fullness, early satiety, epigastric pain/burning
  • >3 months duration with onset >6 months before diagnosis
2.3. IBS-FD Overlap Implications
  • >50% of individuals with IBS also meet criteria for FD
  • Shared pathophysiology mechanisms
  • Disturbances in gut-brain signaling
  • Central sensitization
  • Coexistence of extraintestinal pain disorders supports altered central pain processing
2.4. Diagnostic Testing Recommendations
  • Limited testing sufficient for positive DGBI diagnosis:
  • Serum tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody (celiac)
  • Fecal calprotectin or CRP
  • Complete blood count (CBC)
  • Select testing based on clinical features:
  • Thyroid-stimulating hormone
  • Stool infection (e.g., Giardia)
  • Breath testing
  • Colonoscopy
3. Brain-Gut Axis Model
3.1. Visceral Hypersensitivity Mechanism
  • Altered gut-brain interaction in IBS and FD
  • Leads to increased visceral sensitivity
  • Results in abnormal central pain processing
  • Chronic symptoms occur without structural disease
3.2. Bidirectional Stress Cycle
  • Stress and anxiety ↑ GI symptoms
  • Worsening GI symptoms → ↑ stress and anxiety
  • Creates a bidirectional cycle driving chronic symptoms
  • Stress is not usually the cause of IBS but can amplify symptoms
3.3. Central Sensitization Contributors
  • Neural pathway dysregulation
  • Immune pathway alterations
  • Neuroendocrine pathway disturbances
  • Descending pain-inhibitory pathways dysfunction
  • Amplified peripheral signals at dorsal horn neurons
4. Assessment Domains (Table 1)
4.1. IBS Diagnosis Domain
  • Rome criteria for IBS
  • Symptom pattern assessment
  • Alarm features evaluation
  • Confirms positive diagnosis
  • Reduces unnecessary investigations
  • Validates patient symptoms
4.2. Overlapping DGBI Assessment
  • IBS + FD criteria application
  • Extraintestinal pain evaluation
  • Suggests central sensitization
  • Supports neuromodulator and BGBT use
4.3. Limited Diagnostic Testing
  • CBC, CRP/fecal calprotectin
  • Celiac serology
  • Selective colonoscopy
  • H. pylori testing (for coexistent dyspepsia)
  • Normal results support DGBI diagnosis
  • Reinforces positive diagnosis and care plan
4.4. Food-Related Symptoms Assessment
  • Symptom-food associations
  • Meal timing analysis
  • Fear of symptoms evaluation
  • Differentiates intolerance vs GI symptom anxiety-driven avoidance
  • Guides nutrition and behavioral interventions
4.5. Maladaptive Food Avoidance Behaviors
  • Rigid diet adherence
  • Inadequate nutritional intake
  • Failure to reintroduce foods
  • Social avoidance patterns
  • Fear-driven restriction
  • Weight loss trajectory
  • Loss of enjoyment of eating
4.6. Eating Disorder Screening
  • EDE-Q (Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire)
  • ARFID screen (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder)
  • Intake history review
  • Weight trajectory analysis
  • Detects ARFID risk or restrictive eating patterns
4.7. Food Allergy/Intolerance Evaluation
  • History of food-related urticaria/wheezing
  • IgE allergy testing only for suspected true food allergy
  • Consistent food triggers identification
  • Response to short elimination trials
  • Prevents unnecessary dietary restriction
4.8. Stress-Sensitive Symptoms Assessment
  • Symptom onset/flares associated with increased stressful events
  • Perceived stress measurement
  • Sleep disturbances evaluation
  • Fatigue assessment
  • Suggests autonomic and HPA axis dysregulation
  • Guides mind-body interventions
4.9. Psychological Comorbidity Assessment
  • Anxiety/depression screening
  • GI-specific anxiety evaluation
  • Detects central amplification and avoidance
  • Supports behavioral therapy integration
4.10. Trauma History Assessment
  • Preface with reassurance and permission-based language
  • Key questions:
  • "Have you had difficult or traumatic experiences?"
  • "Do they still affect you today?"
  • Identifies adverse life events and chronic stress
  • Guides trauma-focused care and referral
5. Dietary Management Approach
5.1. Maladaptive Food Avoidance in This Patient
  • Fear-of-symptom-related food avoidance
  • Progressive restriction leading to malnutrition
  • Being underweight with inadequate macronutrient intake
  • Reduced food-related QoL
  • Social isolation and loss of eating enjoyment
  • ARFID consideration warranted
5.2. Distinguishing IBS-Related vs Disordered Eating
  • Food avoidance common in DGBI with meal-related symptoms
  • Not always indicative of eating disorder pathology
  • Clinical history evaluation essential
  • Brief screening tools available (need validation in GI populations)
  • Both weight and non-weight-related eating disorders more prevalent in DGBI
5.3. Diet Stacking Risks
  • Repeated elimination diets increase risk of:
  • Eating disorders
  • Malnutrition
  • Reduced quality of life
  • Signs triggering maladaptive food avoidance screening
5.4. Evidence-Based Dietary Interventions
  • Low-FODMAP diet (fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, polyols)
  • British Dietetic Association NICE guidelines
  • Both show promise for global symptom relief
  • Low starch/sucrose diet → requires further validation
  • Modified FODMAP and Mediterranean diets → require further validation
5.5. Dietary Recommendations for IBS-M
  • Individualized based on predominant/distressing symptoms
  • Improving bowel habits often reduces bloating and pain
  • Soluble fiber (psyllium) for constipation
  • Kiwi or papaya for constipation symptoms
  • Flaxseed supplementation
  • Reassurance and reducing/substituting food triggers
  • Adjusting meal structure and timing
  • Smaller, balanced, frequent meals → may reduce bloating and visceral hypersensitivity
5.6. Nutritional Rehabilitation Approach
  • Dietitian-guided counseling preferred
  • Minimize unnecessary food avoidance
  • Address weight loss and nutritional risk
  • Functional food additions rather than elimination preferred in maladaptive avoidance
  • Gradual reintroduction of previously eliminated foods
5.7. Food Allergy Testing Perspective
  • IgE-based testing evaluates true food allergy (uncommon without urticaria, angioedema, wheezing)
  • Food intolerance best evaluated with short trial of avoidance rather than testing
  • Commercial IgG food sensitivity panels generally not recommended
  • Exception: novel 18-food IBS-specific IgG ELISA-based panel showed efficacy in recent RCT
  • 59.6% met primary abdominal pain endpoint vs 42.1% sham
  • Greater benefits in IBS-C and IBS-M (exploratory findings)
  • Any elimination strategy should be:
  • Time-limited
  • Dietitian-supervised
  • Followed by structured food reintroduction
6. Pharmacological Treatments for IBS-M
6.1. Antispasmodics
  • Peppermint oil (enteric-coated, 180-200 mg three times daily)
  • Well-tolerated
  • Relaxes smooth muscle without significantly affecting bowel habits
6.2. Antidiarrheal Agents
  • Loperamide (peripherally active mu-opioid receptor agonist)
  • Initial dose: low doses to avoid worsening constipation
  • Reduces stool frequency and urgency
  • Does not significantly affect pain
6.3. Constipation Treatments
  • Polyethylene glycol (17 g daily) → improves stool consistency
  • Magnesium oxide (500-1500 mg daily)
  • Senna (8.6-25 mg daily)
  • Soluble fiber (psyllium) → improves stool form
6.4. Secretagogues
  • Linaclotide (290 mcg daily)
  • Plecanatide (3 mg daily)
  • Lubiprostone (8 mcg twice daily)
  • Tenapanor (50 mg twice daily) - NHE3 antagonist
6.5. Microbiome Modulation
  • Rifaximin (500 mg three times daily)
  • Non-absorbable antibiotic
  • This patient had minimal, transient relief with two courses
6.6. Mixed Opioid Receptor Agents
  • Eluxadoline (75-100 mg twice daily)
  • For diarrhea-predominant phases
6.7. Neuromodulators for IBS and FD
6.7.1. Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs)
  • Amitriptyline and imipramine = tertiary amines
  • Greater antimuscarinic, H1 histamine, alpha-1 adrenergic effects
  • Associated with sedation, weight gain, dry mouth
  • May be advantageous in younger patients or those with sleep/weight difficulties
  • Desipramine and nortriptyline = secondary amines
  • Better tolerated in some patients
ATLANTIS Trial Results
  • Low-dose amitriptyline (10-30 mg qhs) vs placebo in moderate-severe IBS
  • All subtypes included
  • Significantly improved IBS symptoms and abdominal pain vs placebo
  • Benefits sustained over 6 months
  • Treatment effects independent of baseline anxiety/depression
  • Supports primary neuromodulatory (not antidepressant) mechanism
6.7.2. Amitriptyline for Functional Dyspepsia
  • Randomized trial: amitriptyline vs escitalopram vs placebo
  • Amitriptyline significantly improved upper abdominal pain and overall symptoms
  • Particularly effective in patients with normal gastric emptying
  • Predominant epigastric pain → best response
  • Escitalopram was not more effective than placebo
6.7.3. SNRIs and Other Options
  • Duloxetine (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor)
  • Dose: 20-60 mg daily
  • Improves chronic pain syndromes (fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue)
  • Has anti-anxiety and antidepressant properties
  • Buspirone (5-HT₁ partial agonist)
  • Reduces FD symptoms
  • Useful in both FD and IBS
  • Mirtazapine (tetracyclic antidepressant)
  • Dose: 7.5-45 mg at bedtime
  • Reduces FD symptoms
  • Useful in both FD and IBS
6.8. Herbal Supplements
  • Enteric-coated peppermint oil (180-200 mg three times daily)
  • For postprandial abdominal pain and loose stools
  • L-glutamine (5 g three times daily)
  • For diarrhea and abdominal pain
  • Targets increased intestinal permeability
6.9. Probiotics
  • Bifidobacterium infantis
  • Multi-strain formulations
  • For global symptoms
7. Brain-Gut Behavioral Therapies (BGBT)
7.1. GI-Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (GI-CBT)
  • Cognitive restructuring techniques
  • Flexible coping strategy development
  • Helps understand relationships between stressors and GI symptoms
  • Addresses hypervigilance and GI-specific anxiety
  • Effective for symptom flares
7.2. Gut-Directed Hypnotherapy
  • Standardized hypnosis protocols
  • Excellent treatment for pain and discomfort
  • Reduces autonomic arousal
  • Increases self-efficacy
  • Effective across DGBI conditions
7.3. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)
  • Values-based interventions
  • Mindfulness techniques
  • Addresses symptom flares and poor quality of life
  • Reduces GI-specific anxiety
7.4. Diaphragmatic Breathing and Relaxation
  • Activates rest-and-digest system
  • Improves autonomic balance through enhanced cardiovagal tone
  • Patients experience physiological shift firsthand
  • Gains practical self-regulation tool
7.5. Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR)
  • 8 weeks of structured mindfulness training
  • Improves:
  • Symptom severity
  • GI-specific anxiety
  • Quality of life (QoL)
  • Benefits last up to 12 months
7.6. Mindfulness Meditation Practice
  • Nonjudgmental awareness of thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations
  • Does not immediately react or try to change sensations
  • Builds distress tolerance and confidence in tolerating discomfort
  • Allows nervous system to reappraise threat
  • Reduces stress reactivity
  • Particularly helpful for:
  • Symptom-related fear
  • Sympathetic arousal
  • Pain catastrophizing
  • Strengthens attention control
  • Reduces amygdala reactivity
7.7. Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy
  • EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing)
  • This patient: resolution of nightmares
  • Improvement in psychological and somatic symptoms
  • Prolonged Exposure Therapy
  • Cognitive Processing Therapy
8. Clinical Decision Tool (Figure 2)
8.1. Initial Patient Assessment
  • Recurrent abdominal pain with altered bowel habits
  • Comprehensive clinical assessment
  • Evaluation for alarm features
8.2. Limited Screening Tests
  • CBC, CRP/fecal calprotectin
  • Celiac serologies
8.3. Alarm Features Present?
  • Yes → Other diseases: treat accordingly
  • No → Proceed to positive IBS diagnosis
8.4. Bowel Habit Subtype Classification
  • IBS-D (diarrhea-predominant)
  • IBS-M (mixed bowel habits)
  • IBS-C (constipation-predominant)
8.5. Management Approach by Subtype
IBS-D Treatment
  • Antispasmodics
  • Antidiarrheals
  • Rifaximin
  • TCAs/SNRIs
  • Eluxadoline
  • 5-HT3 antagonists
IBS-C Treatment
  • Antispasmodics
  • Laxatives (e.g., PEG, MgO)
  • Secretagogues (Linaclotide, Plecanatide, Lubiprostone)
  • NHE3 inhibitor (Tenapanor)
  • TCAs/SNRIs
IBS-M Treatment
  • IBS-D or IBS-C treatment aligned with current predominant bowel pattern
8.6. Referral Considerations
  • Refer to GI dietitian if:
  • Postprandial symptoms present
  • Weight loss observed
  • Suspected disordered eating
  • Nutritional risk identified
  • Refer to GI psychologist if:
  • Cognitive-affective processes affecting GI symptoms
  • GI symptom-related anxiety present
  • Avoidance behaviors identified
9. Case Outcome and Multidisciplinary Approach
9.1. Treatment Components Implemented
  • Patient-centered education
  • Dietary modification (gradual reintroduction)
  • Neuromodulators
  • Trauma-focused therapy (EMDR)
  • Mindfulness-based therapies
9.2. Specific Interventions
  • Low-dose desipramine (10 mg nightly)
  • Improved postprandial urgency and diarrhea
  • Improved food tolerance
  • Magnesium oxide (400 mg capsule at bedtime)
  • Reduced constipation
  • Improved sleep
9.3. Dietary Progress
  • Gradually reintroduced fiber
  • Expanded diet with small amounts of legumes and vegetables
  • Demonstrated improved tolerance
  • Discontinued bowel cleanses, saline infusions, unnecessary supplements
9.4. Trauma Therapy Outcomes
  • EMDR therapy initiated for trauma history
  • Resolution of nightmares
  • Improvement in psychological and somatic symptoms
9.5. Mind-Body Practice Integration
  • Patient identified diaphragmatic breathing and mindfulness as central to recovery
  • Helped tolerate treatment and symptom fluctuations
9.6. Endocrine Adjustments
  • Eventually tapered off hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone
  • Stable thyroid replacement maintained
9.7. Final Outcomes
  • Significant improvement in GI symptoms and function
  • Discontinued desipramine
  • Gradual diet expansion sustained
  • Energy, sleep, and stress resilience improved
  • Sustained symptom control despite ongoing stressors
  • Patient reported regaining "more normal life"
10. Key Clinical Principles
10.1. Diagnostic Framework
  • Negative workup does not negate disease burden
  • Positive diagnosis with symptom pattern validation essential
  • Limited testing supports positive DGBI diagnosis
10.2. Multidisciplinary Team Approach
  • Gastroenterology for diagnosis and medical management
  • GI dietitian for nutritional rehabilitation
  • GI psychologist for cognitive-affective contributors
  • Integrative GI practitioner for mind-body interventions
10.3. Mechanism-Based Care
  • Target visceral hypersensitivity
  • Address stress-related dysregulation
  • Treat overlapping DGBI conditions
  • Restore function, confidence, and resilience
10.4. Patient-Centered Validation
  • Explain brain-gut model without stigmatizing
  • Emphasize biological basis of symptoms
  • Clarify stress-anxiety-symptom bidirectional cycle
  • Build confidence in diagnosis to reduce repeat testing requests
10.5. Trauma-Informed Care
  • Systematic trauma history assessment with all patients
  • Use permission-based language
  • Reassure patients they don't need to provide details
  • Guide trauma-focused care and appropriate referral
10.6. Nutritional Rehabilitation Principles
  • Prefer functional food additions over elimination in maladaptive avoidance
  • Time-limited, dietitian-supervised elimination diets with structured reintroduction
  • Monitor for eating disorder risk throughout treatment
10.7. Pharmacological Considerations
  • TCAs effective for IBS and FD regardless of baseline anxiety/depression
  • Low-dose amitriptyline well-tolerated with sustained benefits over 6 months
  • Treatment effects support neuromodulatory (not antidepressant) mechanism
10.8. Psychological Intervention Sequencing
  • Trauma-focused treatment often most appropriate first
  • BGBT (GI-CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy) can follow or run concurrently
  • Mindfulness and breathing practices support all interventions

12. Multimodal Treatment Summary (IBS-M)
Dietary Interventions
  • Fiber modification: psyllium, kiwifruit → constipation, stool irregularity
  • Low-FODMAP diet: structured elimination and reintroduction → bloating, pain, diarrhea
  • Targeted elimination diets: dairy-free → postprandial symptoms
  • Dietitian-guided counseling: minimize unnecessary food avoidance
Over-the-Counter Medications
  • Loperamide (8.6 mg once or twice daily) → diarrhea-predominant flares
  • Polyethylene glycol (17 g daily) → constipation-predominant flares
  • Magnesium (500-1500 mg daily)
  • Senna (8.6-25 mg daily)
  • Probiotics: Bifidobacterium infantis, multi-strain → global symptoms
  • Enteric-coated peppermint oil (180-200 mg three times daily) → visceral pain
  • L-glutamine (5 g three times daily) → increased intestinal permeability
Prescription Medications
  • Linaclotide (290 mcg daily) → constipation-predominant flares, abdominal pain
  • Plecanatide (3 mg daily) → constipation-predominant flares, abdominal pain
  • Lubiprostone (8 mcg twice daily) → constipation-predominant flares, abdominal pain
  • Tenapanor (50 mg twice daily) → constipation-predominant flares, abdominal pain
  • Rifaximin (500 mg three times daily) → diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating
  • Eluxadoline (75-100 mg twice daily) → diarrhea-predominant phases
  • TCAs: amitriptyline, desipramine (10-50 mg at bedtime) → abdominal pain, extraintestinal symptoms
  • SNRIs: duloxetine (20-60 mg daily) → abdominal pain, extraintestinal symptoms
  • Mirtazapine (7.5-45 mg at bedtime) → abdominal pain, extraintestinal symptoms
Brain-Gut Behavioral Therapies
  • GI-CBT: cognitive restructuring, flexible coping → symptom flares, hypervigilance, GI-specific anxiety
  • ACT: values-based interventions, mindfulness → symptom flares, poor QoL, GI-specific anxiety
  • Gut-directed hypnotherapy: standardized protocols → global symptoms, autonomic dysregulation
  • Relaxation/biofeedback: diaphragmatic breathing, thoraco-abdominal → global symptoms, bloating
  • Mindfulness-based therapy: MBSR, meditation → anxiety-related symptoms
Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy
  • EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing)
  • Prolonged Exposure Therapy
  • Cognitive Processing Therapy
